title: Suicide risk: formulation, not prediction
blurb: Ask about suicide directly, build a risk formulation around needs and safety, and avoid using scores or low/medium/high labels to predict or ration care.
question: Mr Ward, 36, tells his community mental health nurse he has thought about suicide every day this week since his partner left. The team's old form asks for a 'low, medium or high' rating. What should the nurse focus on instead?

teach.body: NICE NG225 says do not use risk assessment tools and scales, or global low, medium or high ratings, to predict suicide or repeat self-harm, or to decide who gets treatment or is discharged. Instead, mental health professionals carry out a risk formulation as part of every psychosocial assessment, focused on the person's needs and how to support their immediate and longer-term safety. In plain English: we cannot forecast who will die, so we understand the person and plan their safety with them.

rows.label: Question
values: Why now, and what keeps them safe?

rows.label: Used to
values: Shape care and a safety plan

teach.caption: Risk tools have poor predictive value; many people who die by suicide were judged low risk at their last contact (NCISH).

head: Factor group
Examples
rows: Past self-harm or attempts, trauma, family history of suicide
Hopelessness, intent, plans, alcohol, relationship loss
Children, faith, reasons for living, support
teach.caption: Enduring (static) factors set a background; dynamic factors change and are where safety plans act.

steps.label: Ask directly
steps.sub: 'Have you had thoughts of ending your life?' (NG222 1.2.8)

steps.label: Thoughts
steps.sub: How often, how intrusive, how long

teach.caption: Asking directly and openly is part of compassionate assessment; it shows the person you can hear it.

items.label: Within 7 days; within 48 h if suicide risk (NG53)

teach.caption: NG53 1.6.6-1.6.8: identify suicide risk with the person and plan follow-up accordingly.

teach.body: Nurse Achebe asks Mr Ward directly about his thoughts, how often they come, whether he has a plan and what has stopped him so far. He has thought about an overdose and has a stockpile of tablets; his daughter is his reason for living. Together they write down what triggers the worst moments (evenings alone), agree he will hand the tablets to his sister, list people and crisis numbers, and arrange a visit within 48 hours. The record describes the formulation and plan, not a risk rating.

teach.text: A 'low risk' label, or a low score on any scale, is not a reason to discharge or withhold care, and a 'high' label does not by itself tell you what to do. NG225 rules out both uses. Also, any sudden, unexplained change in mood or behaviour needs exploring with the person, not assuming it is recovery.

items: Do not use scales or low/medium/high ratings to predict suicide or to decide treatment or discharge (NG225 1.6.1-1.6.4).
Mental health professionals complete a risk formulation in every psychosocial assessment.
Ask directly about thoughts, plans, intent, means and what keeps the person safe.
Explore historic, current, future and protective factors.
After discharge, follow up within 7 days, or within 48 hours if suicide risk has been identified (NG53).

summary: You can now ask directly about suicide, explore historic, current, future and protective factors, and turn them into a shared risk formulation and safety plan. You can also explain why NICE rules out risk scales and low/medium/high ratings for predicting suicide or allocating care.

A.q: Which statement reflects NICE NG225 on risk assessment tools and scales for suicide?
options: They can show who is safe to discharge
They should sort people into low, medium or high
They can predict who will attempt suicide
They should not be used to predict suicide
A.why: NG225 1.6.1-1.6.4: do not use risk tools, scales or global low/medium/high stratification to predict suicide or self-harm, or to decide who is offered treatment or discharged.

whyNot.0: Using scales to decide discharge is explicitly advised against (1.6.2).
whyNot.1: Global stratification into low, medium or high is advised against (1.6.3-1.6.4).
whyNot.2: Scales should not be used to predict suicide (1.6.1).

A.q: Who should undertake a risk formulation as part of every psychosocial assessment after self-harm, according to NICE NG225?
options: The emergency department triage nurse
Mental health professionals
The person's GP within 7 days
The ward healthcare assistant
A.why: NG225 1.6.6: mental health professionals should undertake a risk formulation as part of every psychosocial assessment.

whyNot.0: ED triage establishes immediate needs and refers for psychosocial assessment.
whyNot.2: GPs review and refer, but the formulation is part of the mental health professional's psychosocial assessment.
whyNot.3: Formulation requires mental health professional training (NG225 1.14.3).

A.q: Under NICE NG53, how soon should a person be followed up after discharge from mental health in-patient care if a risk of suicide has been identified?
options: Within 7 days
Within 2 weeks
Within 48 hours
Within 24 hours
A.why: NG53 1.6.8: follow up within 48 hours of discharge if a risk of suicide has been identified (1.6.7: within 7 days for everyone).

whyNot.0: Seven days is the standard for all discharged patients, not where suicide risk is identified.
whyNot.1: Two weeks relates to considering a GP appointment (1.6.2).
whyNot.3: 24 hours is the deadline for the discharge letter to the GP (1.6.3).

B.q: During a psychosocial assessment, Mr Ellis, 55, mentions that his court hearing for a driving offence is next month. Under which NG225 factor group is this best recorded?
options: A historic factor
A future factor
A protective factor
A predisposing factor
B.why: NG225 1.5.10 asks about future factors, including specific upcoming events or circumstances, such as a court date.

whyNot.0: Historic factors are past events such as previous attempts.
whyNot.2: A court hearing is a stressor, not protective.
whyNot.3: Predisposing is a 5 Ps term for long-standing vulnerability, not an upcoming event.

B.q: A newly registered nurse asks why the trust stopped rating patients as 'low, medium or high' suicide risk. Which explanation is best?
options: Ratings predict poorly and many who die were rated low
Ratings take too long to complete on busy wards
Ratings are now done by doctors instead of nurses
Ratings were replaced by a stricter numerical scale
B.why: NICE's rationale for NG225 1.6.1-1.6.4: risk tools and scales cannot accurately predict suicide or self-harm, and stratification wrongly implies risk is static. NCISH 2026: at final contact, immediate risk was judged low or absent in 81% of patients who died by suicide.

whyNot.1: The change is about accuracy and harm, not time.
whyNot.2: NICE advises against stratification by any professional.
whyNot.3: NICE advises against scales for prediction too.

B.q: Mr Byrne, 63, an in-patient with severe depression who has been very distressed for weeks, is suddenly calm and smiling and has given his watch to another patient. What should the nurse do?
options: Record that he is improving and reduce observation
Return the watch and remind him of ward rules
Plan his discharge, as he is now settled
Explore with him now what the change means
B.why: A sudden, unexplained change in a severely depressed in-patient is a change in mental state that must be assessed, not assumed to be recovery. NG222 1.2.8: ask directly about suicidal ideation and intent; NG10 1.4.17: observation levels rest on current mental state and risk assessment. The nurse explores the change with him, reviews the plan and informs the team.

whyNot.0: Reducing observation needs a review of his current mental state and risk (NG10 1.4.17), not an assumption from his smile.
whyNot.1: This deals with the property and leaves an unexplained change in his mental state unassessed.
whyNot.2: Discharge needs a full assessment of his mental state and safety, and early post-discharge weeks carry raised risk (NCISH).

C.q: Mr Ward, 36, says he thinks about suicide every day and has a stockpile of paracetamol at home. His daughter is his reason to live. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Rate his risk as high and arrange admission
Record a low risk because he has a protective factor
Agree a plan with him to make the tablets safe
Give him a crisis number and review in a month
C.why: NG225 1.7.1 and 1.11.7: establish the means and, with therapeutic collaboration, remove or restrict access, as part of a safety plan built from the formulation.

whyNot.0: A global rating does not decide care, and admission is not automatically the least restrictive option.
whyNot.1: One protective factor does not make him low risk, and ratings should not decide care.
whyNot.3: A month's delay ignores current means and daily suicidal thoughts.

C.q: Ms Quinn, 40, is being discharged home after an admission following a suicide attempt. Which follow-up best meets NICE NG53?
options: Follow-up contact within 48 hours
A GP appointment within 2 weeks
Follow-up contact within 7 days
An outpatient review within 4 weeks
C.why: NG53 1.6.8: follow up within 48 hours of discharge where a risk of suicide has been identified; the early post-discharge period carries raised risk.

whyNot.1: A GP appointment within 2 weeks may be considered, but it is not the follow-up standard.
whyNot.2: Seven days is the standard where no suicide risk has been identified.
whyNot.3: Four weeks leaves her unsupported through the highest-risk period.

C.q: Mrs Lowe, 74, attends the emergency department after an overdose of her husband's tablets. She says it was 'a silly mistake' and wants to go home. Which response best follows NICE NG225?
options: Discharge her, as her risk score is low
Refer her to her GP for a routine review
Advise her husband to keep his tablets locked away
Assess her safety and mental health before she leaves
C.why: NG225 1.5.14: if a person wants to leave before a full psychosocial assessment, assess their safety and mental health before they leave; 1.5.12 notes higher suicide rates after self-harm in older people.

whyNot.0: Risk scores must not decide discharge.
whyNot.1: A routine GP review leaves her without the assessment she needs now.
whyNot.2: Restricting means helps but does not replace assessing her safety and mental state.

blocks.body: Swap 'how risky is this person?' for 'what is going on for this person, what makes things worse, what keeps them safe, and what will we do together?' Ask directly about suicide, explore the four factor groups, and build a safety plan the person owns.

blocks.text: A low rating never justifies discharge, and a high rating is not a plan.

explain.body: NG225: do not use risk tools, scales or global low, medium or high stratification to predict suicide or repeat self-harm, or to decide who receives treatment or is discharged.

test.q: A form asks the nurse to rate a patient's suicide risk as low, medium or high to decide discharge. What does NICE NG225 advise?
options: Use the rating, then confirm with the doctor
Rate medium when uncertain, to be cautious
Do not use global ratings for this decision
Use the rating if the patient agrees with it
test.why: NG225 1.6.4: do not use global risk stratification into low, medium or high risk to determine who should be offered treatment or discharged.

whyNot.0: Medical confirmation does not make a prohibited use acceptable.
whyNot.1: A default 'medium' rating is still global stratification.
whyNot.3: Agreement does not make the rating predictive.

explain.body: Ask people directly about suicidal thoughts and intent, then explore plans, preparation, access to means and what has stopped them acting so far.

test.q: Mr Hart says he has thought about ending his life. Which question should the nurse ask next?
options: 'You wouldn't really do that, would you?'
'Have you made any plans to end your life?'
'Shall we talk about something more positive?'
'Have you told your GP about this yet?'
test.why: After disclosure, explore plans, intent and preparation directly and openly (NG222 1.2.8).

whyNot.0: A leading, dismissive question discourages honest disclosure.
whyNot.2: Changing the subject avoids the assessment.
whyNot.3: This shifts focus away from assessing current risk.

explain.body: NG225 1.5.10: explore historic, changeable and current, future and protective or mitigating factors to identify strengths, vulnerabilities and needs.

test.q: A woman's previous suicide attempt five years ago is best recorded as which NG225 factor?
options: A future factor
A protective factor
A current factor
A historic factor
test.why: Past events such as a previous attempt are historic factors (NG225 1.5.10).

whyNot.1: A previous attempt increases risk rather than protecting.
whyNot.2: Current factors are present and changeable, such as hopelessness now.

explain.body: The weeks after leaving hospital carry raised risk. NG53: follow up everyone within 7 days, and within 48 hours if suicide risk has been identified; send the GP a discharge letter within 24 hours.

test.q: Under NICE NG53, how soon should every person discharged from mental health in-patient care be followed up?
options: Within 7 days
Within 14 days
Within 28 days
Within 12 weeks
test.why: NG53 1.6.7: follow up a person who has been discharged within 7 days.

whyNot.1: 14 days is longer than the NG53 standard.
whyNot.2: 28 days is far beyond the NG53 standard.
whyNot.3: 12 weeks is far beyond the NG53 standard.
